01  Figma Annotation Reference
Figma Design Reference
Use the table below to build your 3 graphics in Figma. Each row = one annotation number. The same numbered point covers all 3 graphic types — Before/After, Psychology Map, and Decision Guide — from a different angle.
#
Points to (page element)
Psychology question
Decision guide (what it achieves)
1
Product imageFull-bleed, hip-to-chin crop, no white margins
"Can I clearly see the product on a real body?"
Stronger product focus — optimised crop removes doubt about fit before it forms
2
Star rating + review countMoved above fold, count bold at 13px, tappable
"Do people actually trust and buy this?"
Visible social proof builds instant trust — hidden at 10px it might as well not exist
3
Product name (H1)22px / 800 weight — clear hierarchy above body text
"What exactly is this product?"
Clear product naming improves comprehension — hierarchy tells the eye where to start
4
Benefit statementOne line between product name and colour selector
"Why should I buy this over any other tee?"
Supports the decision with a quick value explanation — earns the micro-commitment before asking for a choice
5
Price + shipping line"Free shipping over $50 · Free returns" in green below price
"What does shipping actually cost? Can I return it?"
Eliminates the #1 cart abandonment reason before checkout — answers both shipping and returns anxiety in one line
6
Colour swatches32px circles with selected-state ring + colour name shown as text
"Which colour should I pick — and did I select the right one?"
Visual variant selection improves UX and speed — selected colour name removes micro-doubt from the choice
7
Size buttons44px height minimum, bold border on selected state, size guide link prominent
"What size am I — and am I selecting the right one?"
Clear selection states reduce hesitation — 44px tap targets cut misclicks and signal confidence
8
Material benefit chips + Add to Cart100% Cotton · Machine Wash · UPF 15+ chips above CTA; full-width navy button at 54px
"What is it made of — and is it worth the price?"
Trust signals and specs surfaced early reduce buying friction — high-contrast CTA drives the action when the buyer is ready
How to use
In Figma, use annotation numbers 1–8 pointing to the same elements across all 3 graphics. Before/After — numbered dots on the After screenshot. Psychology Map — curved arrows from each question to the corresponding element. Decision Guide — curved arrows from each "what it achieves" label to the corresponding element. Column 2 of the table = dot placement target. Column 3 = Psychology label. Column 4 = Decision Guide label.

LinkedIn + Instagram · Customer Psychology
Format: lead with the solution (what the redesign answers), then mention what was there before. Not problem-first.
Your customer lands on your product page with 8 questions. Here's how the redesign answered every single one: "How does it look?" → Full-bleed image, proper crop. Buyers now see the fit on a real body — not a chest-only shot with dead margins on both sides. "Do people trust this?" → Reviews with count now readable above the fold. Before: stars only, count invisible at 10px. "What exactly is this?" → Product name at 22px bold with a one-line benefit statement below it. Clear hierarchy, no guessing. "Is it worth the price?" → Material chips (100% cotton, UPF 15+) visible above the CTA. Before: buried in an accordion three scrolls down. "What does shipping cost?" → Free shipping line in green, below the price. Before: not mentioned until checkout. "Which size am I?" → 44px size buttons with a clear selected state and a prominent size guide link. Before: underheight tap targets, no guide visible. "Will this fit me?" → Fit selector (Regular/Slim/Relaxed) clearly labelled with selected state shown. "Should I buy now?" → CTA full-width, high contrast, always in reach. Before: below the fold on first load. The page had all the right ingredients. It just wasn't answering the right questions. LinkedIn + Instagram · Decision Guide
Format: bold principle → element-by-element explanation of what each change achieves for the buyer's decision.
High-converting pages don't guess what the buyer needs. They answer every question before it becomes a reason to leave. Here's what each element in this Eddie Bauer redesign is actually doing for the buyer's decision: Full-bleed image → answers "how does it fit on a real body?" before the buyer has to wonder. Doubt about fit is the number one reason people don't add clothing to cart. Readable review count → "do people trust this brand?" answered in 0.3 seconds. Hidden at 10px, that proof might as well not exist. Benefit statement → answers "why this tee?" before asking "which colour?" You earn the micro-commitment before you ask for it. Shipping line in green → "what does shipping cost?" killed at the top, not at checkout. One line removes the #1 cart abandonment reason. Material chips above CTA → "is this worth it?" answered by the specs — 100% cotton, UPF 15+, machine wash. Not hidden. Not something they hunt for. Larger size buttons → "am I selecting the right size?" is a confidence question. A 44px button with a clear selected state is an interface people trust. Design isn't decoration. It's direction. Every element either earns its place or it doesn't. Twitter/X · 3 Single Tweets
VARIATION 1 — THE RULE
Your review count is invisible. Your shipping cost is unknown until checkout. Your CTA is below the fold. The product is fine. The page is costing you sales.
VARIATION 2 — THE CONTRAST
Before: reviews invisible, CTA below fold, no shipping info, image cropped wrong. Buyer bounces. After: same product. Same price. Every question answered above the fold. Buyer adds to cart. The page is the difference. Not the product.
VARIATION 3 — THE HOT TAKE
Unpopular opinion: most Shopify stores don't have a traffic problem. They have a page problem. Fix the page first. Then spend on ads.
